lines.orig: Same model, same data, same 1,000 steps. Only one number changed: the learning rate. And it decides everything.
lines.visuals: Real validation-loss curves of TinyGPT trained 1000 steps with AdamW at 7 learning rates (1e-4 … 0.1): lr 1e-4 → 1.74, lr 3e-4 → 0.81, lr 1e-3 → 0.66, lr 3e-3 → 0.55, lr 0.01 → 0.55, lr 0.03 → 1.13, lr 0.1 → 3.72.

lines.orig: Picture the loss as a landscape and the weights as a ball. The gradient is the slope under the ball. Step downhill by the learning rate times the slope. Repeat.
lines.visuals: Toy 1-D loss landscape (illustration) with a yellow ball, an orange tangent showing the slope, and the update rule w ← w − lr × slope; the ball takes 8 steps downhill.

lines.orig: Too small: you crawl. Just right: you settle in a few steps. Too big: every step overshoots, bouncing higher and higher.
lines.visuals: Three toy bowls (illustration): too small (creeps), just right (settles), too big (overshoots, bouncing out of the valley).

lines.orig: The real runs agree. Learning rate one e minus four is still crawling at 1.74. three e minus three reaches 0.55. At 0.1, it thrashes around and ends at 3.72.
lines.visuals: Real AdamW validation curves: lr 1e-4 (too small) ends at 1.74, lr 3e-3 (best) ends at 0.55, lr 0.1 (too big) ends at 3.72.

lines.orig: Loss landscapes often have long, narrow valleys. Plain gradient descent zigzags across the walls and creeps along the floor. Momentum adds up past gradients: the back-and-forth parts cancel, and the steady downhill part builds speed.
lines.visuals: Toy 2-D elongated valley (illustration, contour ellipses), same learning rate 0.19 for both. Top: plain gradient descent zigzags for all 30 steps and ends 1.41 from the minimum; bottom: with momentum (β=0.5, v = 0.5·v + gradient) the zigzag dies out within ~8 steps and it ends 0.32 from the minimum.

lines.orig: On the real model, the best plain SGD ends at 0.74. With momentum, 0.57, at a lower learning rate, since momentum sums gradients.
lines.visuals: Real runs, best learning rate of each: SGD (lr 1) → 0.74, SGD + momentum 0.9 (lr 0.3) → 0.57.

lines.orig: Here's the catch. At step zero, typical gradient sizes differ 274 times between weight tensors. One learning rate can't suit them all.
lines.visuals: Real per-weight gradient size (RMS of the gradient) for 8 of TinyGPT's tensors at initialisation, log scale: from 7.1e-05 (blocks.0.ln1.weight) to 1.9e-02 (blocks.0.attn_out.bias), a 274× spread.

lines.orig: Adam keeps two running averages for every weight: the gradient, which is momentum, and the gradient squared. Dividing one by the square root of the other gives each weight its own step size.
lines.visuals: Adam's update: step = lr × avg(gradient) / √avg(gradient²). Top term = momentum (smoothed direction); bottom = each weight's own typical gradient size, so each weight moves at most about lr per step. PyTorch defaults β1 0.9, β2 0.999, + ε.

lines.orig: AdamW adds weight decay, a small shrink of every weight each step, applied directly to the weights. In this one sweep its good range spans 10 times; momentum SGD's, 3; plain SGD never got close. That forgiveness is a big reason it's the usual default.
lines.visuals: Grid of every real sweep run (learning rate → final val loss). Teal boxes are within 25% of the best (0.68): AdamW 3/7, SGD+momentum 2/4, SGD 0/4.

lines.orig: Our real recipe also uses a schedule: warm up for 100 steps while Adam's averages are still noisy, then decay along a cosine so the model settles. The sweep kept the rate constant on purpose.
lines.visuals: Real learning-rate schedule of the shipped TinyGPT recipe (train/train.py): linear warm-up over 100 steps to 0.003, then cosine decay to 0 at step 3000; plus gradient clipping at norm 1.0. The sweep in this video used a constant rate instead.

lines.orig: So: start with AdamW, sweep the learning rate in steps of three, warm up then decay, and if the loss spikes, turn it down.
lines.visuals: Recap pills: start with AdamW; sweep the learning rate ×3 at a time; warm up, then decay; loss spikes → lower it.
